title: Interregion resilience orchestration and cache warmup plan
summary: Deep technical session focused on orchestrating policy-based multi-region routing, graceful failover, and KV cache warmup for low-latency inference in VPC/private deployments. Covered routing tiers, capacity thresholds, cache replication vs prefix-warmup, quantization tradeoffs, and an ops playbook for runbook drills.
topics: KV cache warmup and eviction strategies
batching and QoS for mixed workloads
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, then jump into the routing policy diagram in slide deck (link shared in chat).
[00:18] Carlos (Customer): Thanks, Maya. We have Priya and Samir here. We're primarily focused on keeping sub-200ms p99 for our triage service, and we want clear failover when a region loses GPU capacity.
[00:35] Rohit (SE): Great, we'll walk through three routing tiers: primary-local, cost-fallback, and geo-fallback. The policy engine can be configured per-route.
[00:50] Priya: When you say primary-local, does that mean sticky session to a region until KV cache eviction? We can't afford cache thrash.
[01:05] Rohit: Right, sticky by default for short sessions. But you can set a sticky-window in seconds — 30 to 120s works well. We also add a soft-eviction signal: if KV hit-rate < 70% and latency climbs, start probabilistic reroute.
[01:30] Samir: What telemetry do we need to detect 'latency climbs'? CPU/GPU queue depth? Mix?
[01:40] Rohit: We ingest token latency, queue depth, GPU utilization, and KV hit-rate. Policy rules are threshold-based and time-windowed to avoid flapping. Example: if p95 token latency > 250ms for 30s AND queue depth > 20 then mark region degraded.
[02:05] Maya: Note: we'll attach the policy JSON examples after the call.
[02:12] Carlos: Can we do canary traffic to a cold replica without priming the full cache?
[02:20] Rohit: Yes. We recommend a two-step warmup: 1) prefix prefetch for high-frequency prompts, 2) synthetic warmup where small traffic is mirrored to the replica to build KV entries. Avoid full-scale priming unless you can afford the tokens.
[02:45] Priya: Mirror vs replicate KV: is there an active replication mechanism? We run VPC private deployment, so cross-region replication is internal to our infra.
[02:58] Rohit: For Private deployments, we provide hooks — you can enable a lightweight async replication agent, but it's intentionally opt-in because of data residency and bandwidth costs. Many customers prefer prefix-warmup + small mirrored traffic.
[03:20] Samir: Any guidance on sizing warmup traffic? We have 300 req/s baseline with bursty peaks to 2k.
[03:30] Rohit: Warmup traffic should be proportional to unique prefix cardinality. Empirically, 5-10% mirrored traffic over 5-10 minutes primes most hot KV keys. For very bursty workloads, consider staggered warmup across subregions.
[03:52] Maya: Let's talk batching and QoS — BlueRiver runs mix of short chat queries and long document generations, yes?
[04:02] Carlos: Correct. Chat is latency-sensitive, doc-gen is throughput-oriented.
[04:08] Rohit: We use dynamic priority queues. Latency-sensitive routes have smaller max-batch and preemptive slots. Doc-gen can be batched aggressively and run on dedicated capacity pools. Routing policy can send doc-gen to a cost-tier region automatically.
[04:30] Priya: How do you prevent a cost-tier take over during regional outage? If primary is down, we can't suddenly flood the cost region with doc-gen and starve chat.
[04:42] Rohit: We implement global QoS quotas: chat priority always reserved tokens at the cluster level. If cost-region starts filling, the router enforces per-tenant bandwidth caps and preemption rules.
[04:55] Samir: Quantization differences can affect logits ordering; will fallbacks to a quantized variant change output enough to break our downstream logic?
[05:07] Rohit: Good point. We recommend runtime-compatible variants: same model family with matched tokenizer and deterministic sampling seed when doing rollbacks. Also attach eval suites to flag semantic regressions. Our rollbacks can be configured to only use quantized fallback for low-risk routes (embeddings, summarization) and avoid for hallucination-sensitive tasks.
[05:34] Carlos: VPC networking concerns — if we send mirrored warmup traffic cross-region, we need to ensure egress costs and compliance.
[05:44] Maya: We'll include a decision matrix: replicate vs warmup vs no-cross-region based on data sensitivity, cost, and latency needs.
[05:55] Priya: Can you walk through the DR runbook steps? We need operationally simple guidance for our on-call.
[06:04] Rohit: Sure. High-level DR playbook: detection -> degrade -> reroute -> warmup -> scale -> validate -> rollback. Each step has human and automated actions.
[06:18] Rohit: Example detection: automated alert if p95 token latency > 250ms AND KV hit-rate drop > 25% for 1 minute. Degrade: shift sensitive traffic to canary fallback at 10-20% to verify behavior. Reroute: if canary passes, increase to 50%, then full. Warmup: start prefix prefetch + 5% mirrored traffic. Scale: autoscale dedicated pool if capacity available. Validate: run smoke prompt set from the eval suite (~50 prompts) and check semantic metrics. Rollback: if semantic drift detected, fallback to previous model variant or reduce traffic.
[07:15] Carlos: Who owns the human decisions? Our SRE or Redwood on-call?
[07:21] Maya: Typically customer SRE owns initial mitigation. Redwood SEs can be on-call for the pilot period or under enterprise support. We'll document escalation paths.
[07:32] Priya: For private installs, are there special hooks for your health signals? We can't push telemetry out of our VPC.
[07:41] Rohit: We support a pull-model: customers can export metrics to a secure bucket or our private agent can push to your internal telemetry. No traffic leaves without your consent.
[07:55] Samir: A corner case: split-brain during partial network partition — two regions believe they own the same sticky sessions. How are kv caches reconciled?
[08:08] Rohit: We avoid active-active ownership for a single session. We use leader-based routing: session tokens are region-anchored. If partition occurs, the policy will mark the minority partition degraded and reroute new sessions. For existing sessions in minority, we rely on stale-cache fallbacks and include TTL-based revalidation. Reconciliation is eventual — we recommend session migration only after leader election completes.
[08:45] Maya: Let's surface an ops playbook snippet: step-by-step runbook for a regional GPU outage (we'll paste it into the doc).
[08:53] Rohit: 1) Pager triggers, 2) Confirm degraded using p95/queue/kv metrics, 3) Set policy to canary fallback at 15%, 4) Monitor smoke tests for 5 minutes, 5) Ramp to 50% then 100% while running warmup.
[09:20] Carlos: What about warmup cost accounting — will those tokens be billed?
[09:27] Maya: Yes, warmup consumes tokens; for pilots we typically offset with credits or a separate warmup allowance in commercial terms. We'll put options in the pricing note.
[09:40] Priya: Action items: we need a concrete policy JSON, recommended warmup script, and a short SRE runbook.
[09:49] Maya: Agreed. We'll share policy templates and a reference script for mirrored warmup.
[09:56] Rohit: Quick note on probe traffic: use low-entropy prompts to ensure high KV hit probability during warmup. Avoid rare tokens.
[10:10] Carlos: Can we have a periodic dry-run exercise to test failover without impacting production?
[10:16] Rohit: Yes — we support traffic shadowing and a 'failover rehearsal' mode that only affects mirrored traffic. We'll provide a rehearsal checklist.
[10:27] Priya: How do we handle client SDK retries during failover to avoid duplicate inferences?
[10:35] Rohit: Use idempotency keys for non-idempotent ops; for streaming queries, the router can send a control message indicating partial-result and resume token. We'll share SDK hints.
[10:50] Samir: Any constraints with model kv cache when the fallback model has different KV shapes due to quantization?
[10:58] Rohit: That's why we recommend model-variant compatibility testing. KV shapes can differ — prefer fallback variants with the same architecture and KV layout. If not possible, treat fallback as stateless and rely on prefix warmup to reduce latency impact.
[11:22] Maya: We're at about 11 minutes, we can speed through the attached checklist and then open Q&A.
[11:29] Rohit: Quick checklist items: policy JSON, warmup script, smoke prompt set, escalation contacts, and rehearsal schedule.
[11:40] Carlos: Thanks. Quick Q: will warmup scripts work in air-gapped on-prem?
[11:46] Rohit: Yes — scripts run locally. For air-gapped, you run synthetic warmup jobs that simulate the mirrored traffic. We provide containerized tooling.
[12:00] Priya: Any recommendations for autoscaling cooldowns during failover? We saw oscillations during a previous outage.
[12:10] Rohit: Longer cooldowns (90–180s) plus hysteresis on scale-down helps. Also coordinate application-level signal: do not scale down until KV hit-rate recovers above a threshold.
[12:28] Samir: For observability, can we get token-level traces correlated with session IDs?
[12:34] Maya: Yes, we can supply tracing hooks and a small tracer library. It will include session-id, model-variant, token-times. We'll provide an instrumentation guide.
[12:48] Carlos: Anything else from Redwood we should expect after this call?
[12:52] Maya: We'll send the policy templates, a cost/benefit matrix for replicate vs warmup, a sample warmup script, and a proposed rehearsal date.
[13:05] Priya: Sounds good. We'll schedule a follow-up ops runbook walkthrough.
[13:12] Maya: Great. Thank you everyone. We'll capture action items in the notes and follow up with the attachments.
[13:20] End of recording.
